{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Benjamin Abram Bernstein''' (20 May 1881, [[Pasvalys]], [[Lithuania]] – 25 September 1964, [[Berkeley, California]]) was an American mathematician, specializing in [[mathematical logic]].<ref name=BerkeleyObit>[http://texts.cdlib.org/view?docId=hb338nb1j4&doc.view=frames&chunk.id=div00004&toc.depth=1&toc.id= Benjamin Abram Bernstein, University of California: In Memoriam, April 1965]</ref>

==Biography==
With his Jewish<ref name=runes>{{cite book|title=The Hebrew Impact on Western Civilization|last=Runes|first=Dagobert D.|location=New York|publisher=Philosophical Library|year=1951|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SAX4CAAAQBAJ|isbn=978-1-5040-1296-6}}</ref> family, Bernstein immigrated as a child to the United States. After completing public primary education in 1897 in Baltimore, he completed in 1902 his secondary education at [[Baltimore City College]], and then received in 1905 his A.B. degree from [[Johns Hopkins University]]. After completing two years of graduate study at Johns Hopkins University, he became in 1907 an instructor and continuing graduate student in mathematics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. There he received in 1913, with supervisor [[Mellen W. Haskell]], his Ph.D.<ref name=MathGenRef>{{MathGenealogy|id=23961}}</ref> At Berkeley, Bernstein became in 1918 an assistant professor, in 1923 an associate professor, and in 1928 a full professor of mathematics, retiring in 1951 as professor emeritus.<ref name=BerkeleyObit/>

{{blockquote|When Professor Bernstein began his studies in mathematics, the subject of algebra of logic, or mathematical logic, was just beginning to receive intensive scholarly study, mainly from philosophers. Along with [[Edward Vermilye Huntington|E. V. Huntington]] of Harvard, Professor Bernstein was a pioneer in this field from the mathematical point of view. ... During this early period in the history of mathematical logic, a notable event for the subject was the publication of ''[[Principia Mathematica]]'', by [[Alfred North Whitehead|Whitehead]] and [[Bertrand Russell|Russell]]. Professor Bernstein was an intensive and critical student of this ''Principia'' and discussed it in many papers.<ref name=BerkeleyObit/>}}

He was an Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians|ICM]] in 1924 in Toronto.<ref>Bernstein, B. A. [http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1924.1/Main/icm1924.1.0207.0216.ocr.pdf "Modular representations of finite algebras."] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160924130350/http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1924.1/Main/icm1924.1.0207.0216.ocr.pdf |date=2016-09-24 }} In Proc. 7th Int. Cong. Math, vol. 1, pp. 207-216. 1924.</ref> He was elected in 1931 a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Historic Fellows|website=American Association for the Advancement of Science|url=https://www.aaas.org/fellows/historic}}</ref> His doctoral students include Robert Levit<ref name=MathGenRef/><ref>[http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/sfgate/obituary.aspx?n=robert-levit&pid=143215693 Robert Levit Obituary, San Francisco Chronicle, 30 May 2010]</ref> and [[J.C.C. McKinsey]].

In June 1920 in New York City, Professor Bernstein married Rose Davidson; her brother was the sculptor [[Jo Davidson]]. Bernstein was predeceased by his wife and upon his death was survived by a daughter and a granddaughter.<ref name=BerkeleyObit/>
